transcript.text: Our Henry has gone a bit weak and sounds rough, sort of rattly growl instead of the normal hum. It's about 12 years old. Bags and filter are new. Worth fixing?

It may well be worth fixing, but not until the airflow path has been ruled out. A Henry that has become weak and growly can be partly blocked, and that restriction makes the motor sound much harsher. If the whole airway is clear, the rough growl on a 12-year-old machine makes worn motor bearings/brushes or the motor fan the more likely repair. 1. Unplug it. Remove the hose, tubes and floorhead, then look through each section and the inlet into the machine. Check for a lodged sock, paper, plastic or compacted dust. A coin dropped into a clear tube should pass straight through.
2. Turn the floorhead over and remove hair or thread from the brush bar; it should turn freely by hand. Also check the hose for splits. A blockage or jam found here is usually a cheap, worthwhile fix. If all of that is clear and the suction remains weak with the same rattly growl, stop using it if the noise is getting louder or there is a hot/burning smell. The motor assembly is then the likely issue and would need an engineer or competent repairer to assess. A motor repair can still be worthwhile on a Henry because they are generally repairable, but compare the quoted cost against a replacement before authorising it.
[Helpful to see: image "Poor suction — what to check first" — Lost suction is usually a full bin, a dirty filter or a blockage in the hose, tube or floor head — check and clear those before suspecting the motor. Switch off and unplug first. Typical layout — your model may differ.]

Thank you. I dropped a coin through the hose and it went straight through, so that seems clear. Suction is weak at both the hose end and the head. You mentioned a burning smell: now that you say it, there is a hot, electrical sort of smell after about five minutes of running. I haven't looked at the brush bar, I'm afraid.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Do not use it again until it has been checked by a qualified repairer. Weak suction even directly at the hose, a rough growl and a hot electrical smell together point most strongly to the main motor: commonly worn brushes or bearings, sometimes a damaged motor fan. The floorhead/brush bar would not explain weak suction at the hose end. One final owner-safe check is worthwhile, with the plug out: remove the hose and bag, inspect the inlet just inside the machine and the bag compartment for something drawn in, and make sure the bag collar and filter are properly seated. If that is clear, it reinforces a motor fault rather than an airflow issue. Given the smell, even finding hair on the brush bar would not make it safe to resume using it. A repairer can assess the motor and quote before work. At about 12 years old, a motor repair may still be worthwhile on a Henry if the quote is sensible, but compare the total fitted cost with a replacement.

Worn motor bearings, carbon brushes or motor fan (medium)
